<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, the project is Prawn—a Ruby gem that acts as a PDF generation library. The purpose is to let developers programmatically create PDFs (with drawing, text, image, and security capabilities) using pure Ruby. Your system design diagram should thus focus on depicting the internal components that work together to turn Ruby instructions into PDF content.

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Core Engine (Document Creation): Represent Prawn::Document as the heart of PDF generation.
   • Text Rendering: Include the text layer (modules under lib/prawn/text and its subdirectories for box, formatted text, and inline formatting).
   • Graphics and Drawing: Represent the graphics components (modules under lib/prawn/graphics) that handle vector drawing, colors, lines, curves, and transformations.
   • Fonts and Encoding: Depict the submodules in lib/prawn/fonts (such as for AFM, TTF, OTF, etc.) along with font metric caching.
   • Image Handling: Illustrate the image modules (lib/prawn/images, including specific handling for JPG and PNG).
   • Security: Include components from lib/prawn/security that manage encryption and permissions.
   • Auxiliary Utilities: Indicate supporting modules such as measurements, transformations (like transformation_stack), and utility functions.
   • Manual & Documentation: As a separate documentation component, show the manual directory which contains examples and usage guides. This helps understand external API consumption.
   • Tests and Benchmarks: You might also note the spec and bench directories to capture the testing framework, especially if considering maintenance or extension points.

2. Relationships and Interactions:
   • Start with the Client/Entry Point: At the highest level, the API (via require "prawn" and Prawn::Document.generate method) is initiated.
   • Arrow from the Document component to sub-modules (“calls into” text, graphics, fonts, image_handler, etc.).
   • Show how the Text Engine interacts with Fonts and Encodings: Directional flow from text formatting to proper font rendering.
   • Indicate how the Graphics Engine communicates with the low-level PDF object generation (transparency, blending, patterns, etc.).
   • Include directional arrows showing that images are processed (via image_handler) and then inserted into the document.
   • Illustrate the Security module’s connection to the document finalization process for encryption and permission setup.

3. Design Patterns and Architectural Choices:
   • Layered/MVC-like Approach: The application segregates concerns (rendering text, images, vector graphics) much like an MVC where the “model” (PDF object tree) is built from these independent modules.
   • Modularity: Components such as fonts, graphics, and texts are broken into dedicated modules (each in its pertinent directory) to promote separation of concerns.
   • Extension Points: Note that some modules (e.g., text formatting and inline rendering) have extension methods (hooks for custom behaviors), so include a note in the diagram.

4. Relevant Technologies & Libraries:
   • Ruby as the primary programming language.
   • Use of RubyGems for distribution (indicate that Prawn is installed as a gem).
   • Test frameworks (Rspec as seen in .rspec configuration and the spec directory).
   • Markdown / Rake usage for building the manual and running tests.
   • External dependency on PDF specifications as a design constraint.

5. Guidelines for Drawing the Diagram:
   • Use distinct shapes or colors: For example, use rectangles for core modules (Document, Text, Graphics, Fonts, Images, Security) and ellipses for utility components.
   • Clearly label each component: Write “Prawn::Document” for the central PDF generation engine, “Text (Prawn::Text)” for text processing, and so on.
   • Use directional arrows: Indicate the flow of data and dependencies (e.g., Document → Text, Document → Graphics, Text → Fonts, etc.).
   • Include annotations: Next to each arrow or box, you may include brief notes (e.g., “Processes inline formatting,” “Handles vector drawing commands,” “Manages encryption and permissions”).
   • Consider grouping: Cluster related modules (e.g., all font-related files in one section, all image-related in another) to provide clarity.

6. Tailoring the Diagram for this Project:
   • Focus on separation of functionality rather than front–back division since it’s a library rather than a full-stack web app.
   • Emphasize internal data flow from a high-level API call (i.e., Prawn::Document.generate) to detailed subcomponents (text rendering, image processing, graphics drawing, and security).
   • Highlight transformation and integration points where low-level PDF object creation meets higher-level abstractions.
   • For each module in lib/prawn (and its subdirectories such as document, graphics, fonts, text, images), represent the interaction with drawing commands and layout mechanisms.

7. Final Diagram Elements:
   • Main Entry: A top-level box representing the API that is used by client code.
   • Subcomponents: Arrange separate boxes for Document, Text, Graphics, Fonts, Images, Security, and Utilities.
   • Arrows: Show directional data flow and dependencies between these components.
   • Legend: Create a legend for symbols and colors used (for example, blue for core modules, green for utility modules).
   • Extendability: Optionally include a side-box that shows “Extensions/Manual” to guide integration and reference for developers.

By following these guidelines, your system design diagram will capture the essential architectural elements of the Prawn PDF generation library, clearly demonstrating how Ruby code is translated into a structured PDF document via its modular components. This detailed representation will help in understanding dependencies, data flow, and areas where the system might be extended or maintained.
</explanation>
